root_causes.description: Schema declares no secondary indexes for the lookup and sort columns used by every handler
Reads use entity graphs with multiple collection joins instead of narrow projections
Result sets returned to callers have no server-enforced bound
Synchronous database call in async handler
Transaction wrapped around every request regardless of read/write
Write path issues per-item round trips

findings.problem: The model declares no index on Article.Slug, Person.Username, Person.Email or Article.CreatedAt, yet nearly every handler filters or sorts on them, so each lookup is a table scan as data grows.
findings.performance_principle: Lookups by a non-key attribute must be satisfied by an access path whose cost is sublinear in table size.

evidence.statement: OnModelCreating configures only composite keys and foreign keys for ArticleTag, ArticleFavorite, FollowedPeople; no HasIndex anywhere (a repo-wide search for Index/HasIndex in src found nothing).
Schema is created via EnsureCreated from the model, with no migrations, so the model is the only place an index could be declared.
Article lookups by Slug: Details, Comments List/Create, Favorites, Edit, Delete (e.g. Details.cs FirstOrDefaultAsync x.Slug == ...).
Person lookups by Username on every authenticated write/read (Create article, Comments Create, Favorites Add, Followers, ProfileReader, feed) and by Email on login.
Article list orders by CreatedAt desc, ArticleId desc with Skip/Take.

findings.conditions: Matters once the Articles or Persons tables grow beyond what fits comfortably in cache pages; no row counts are supplied, so the threshold is unknown (assumed: production-sized data, not demo data). SQLite and SQL Server both scan without an index (uniqueness of these columns is only by application convention).

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for HasIndex/[Index]/migrations/raw SQL DDL; found none. Primary keys and FK indexes (ArticleTag, ArticleFavorite composite keys; FK columns) exist implicitly, which covers join paths but not the lookups above.

findings.recommendation: Declare indexes in OnModelCreating: unique on Person.Username, unique on Person.Email, unique on Article.Slug, and an index on Article.CreatedAt (descending, with ArticleId) for the list ordering. Unique indexes also remove the application-level race on slug/username uniqueness checks.
findings.trade_offs: Slower writes and more storage per index; unique indexes can fail on pre-existing duplicate data and require a cleanup step; EnsureCreated will not alter an existing database, so a migration is needed.

validation.metric: Query plan for WHERE Slug=@p and WHERE Username=@p, plus p95 latency of GET /api/articles/{slug}
validation.expectation: Plan changes from table scan to index seek; latency becomes flat with table size
validation.falsifier: Plans already show index seeks (e.g. indexes added out of band) or latency does not vary with row count

commands.command: sqlite3 realworld.db "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM Articles WHERE Slug = 'x';"  -- run against a copy of the database
commands.purpose: Show whether the slug lookup scans (SQLite)

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: At demo or small scale the tables fit in memory and scans are cheap; the app also does not enforce unique usernames/slugs by index, so adding unique indexes has a data-migration cost.

alternatives.option: Declare indexes in the model (preferred): removes scans at the source

alternatives.why: masks the scan and adds invalidation cost

findings.problem: GetAllData Includes Author, ArticleFavorites and ArticleTags in a single non-split query, so each article row is repeated favorites x tags times; the list handler also loads full bodies only to null them afterwards.
findings.performance_principle: Do not multiply result rows by joining independent one-to-many relations in one query; fetch only the columns the response uses.

evidence.statement: Two sibling collection Includes in one query with no AsSplitQuery configured (UseSqlite/UseSqlServer called without query splitting options).
List loads full Article rows (including Body), then sets article.Body = null before returning.
Favorite entities are loaded in full only to compute FavoritesCount/Favorited from the collection count.
Used by List, Details, Favorites Add/Delete.

findings.conditions: Matters when articles accumulate many favorites and several tags each; for a page of 20 articles the cost is the sum of per-article favorites x tags. Favorite counts are unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for AsSplitQuery/QuerySplittingBehavior in Program.cs and the context; none found.
Tags per article are typically few, which bounds the multiplier on one side.

findings.recommendation: Project only the fields the response needs (including FavoritesCount via a subquery COUNT and tag names), or use AsSplitQuery; skip Body in the list projection rather than load and null it.
findings.trade_offs: Projection duplicates mapping logic away from the domain type serialized today; split queries add round trips (a transaction is present, so consistency is kept).

validation.metric: Row count returned by the list SQL for a page, and p95 of GET /api/articles
validation.expectation: Rows per page drop from sum(favorites x tags) toward the page size
validation.falsifier: Logged SQL already shows one row per article

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Typical articles have a handful of tags and tens of favorites; with default page size 20 the extra rows may be negligible compared to network and serialization.

alternatives.option: Select into a DTO projection (preferred): removes both row multiplication and body transfer
AsSplitQuery: fixes multiplication but still loads favorites rows and bodies

findings.problem: Limit and Offset come straight from the query string and are passed to Take/Skip with no upper bound, so one request can ask for the whole table.
findings.performance_principle: Every result set returned to a caller must have a server-enforced upper bound.

evidence.statement: Take(message.Limit ?? 20) and Skip(message.Offset ?? 0) with no clamp or validator on Query.
No validator is defined for the List Query; the controller passes the parameters through.
A large Offset also forces the database to read and discard Offset rows (offset pagination).

findings.conditions: Reachable by any client; matters whenever the Articles table is larger than a page, including accidental clients that set a huge limit.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for Math.Min/clamps, a max-page-size option and a validator on List.Query; none found.

findings.recommendation: Clamp Limit to a documented maximum (and reject negatives) in a Query validator; consider keyset pagination on (CreatedAt, ArticleId) if deep offsets are expected.
findings.trade_offs: Clients relying on very large limits break; keyset pagination changes the RealWorld spec shape.

validation.metric: Response size and DB rows read for GET /api/articles?limit=100000 against a seeded database
validation.expectation: Result is clamped to the maximum
validation.falsifier: Endpoint already returns at most the cap

commands.command: curl -s "http://localhost:5000/api/articles?limit=100000" | wc -c  -- run against a local seeded instance
commands.purpose: Measure response size for an oversized limit

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If an API gateway enforces query-string limits, the cap may exist upstream; none is visible in the repository.

alternatives.why: minimal and removes the unbounded case
also fixes deep-offset cost but changes the API contract

findings.problem: ArticlesCount is computed with the synchronous queryable.Count(), blocking a thread-pool thread during the database call, and runs a second query over the same filtered set.
findings.performance_principle: Do not block threads on I/O in a request path that is otherwise non-blocking.

evidence.statement: queryable.Count() inside an async method, while the page itself uses ToListAsync.

findings.conditions: Matters under high concurrent list traffic with a slow COUNT (large Articles tables, no index on filter columns); negligible at low concurrency.

counter_evidence.statement: The SQLite provider is effectively synchronous underneath, so the async benefit differs by provider; SQL Server is the case where it matters.

findings.recommendation: Use await queryable.CountAsync(cancellationToken) and issue the count without the Includes.

validation.metric: Thread-pool queue length / thread count during a list load test
validation.expectation: No blocked threads attributable to the handler
validation.falsifier: No change in thread-pool metrics under load

findings.problem: Comments List loads the whole article and every comment with its author in one query and returns all of them; Tags List returns every tag. Neither paginates, and Comments Create also loads all existing comments just to add one.
findings.performance_principle: Every result set returned to a caller must have a server-enforced upper bound.

evidence.statement: Articles.Include(Comments).ThenInclude(Author) loads the full article (including Body) plus all comments, tracked, and returns article.Comments.
Tags.OrderBy(TagId).ToListAsync() with no limit.
Comments Create Includes all existing comments to add one.

findings.conditions: Matters for articles with large comment threads (hot articles) and as the tag vocabulary grows; sizes unknown (assumed: production-sized data).

counter_evidence.statement: The upstream RealWorld spec does not paginate comments or tags, which explains the design and limits what can change without breaking clients.

findings.recommendation: Query comments directly (Comments.Where(ArticleId).AsNoTracking() with projection) instead of loading the article; in Create, check article existence without loading comments; add a server-side cap or optional paging for comments and tags.
findings.trade_offs: A cap changes behavior for very large threads; direct queries need a separate existence check.

validation.metric: Rows read and bytes returned for GET comments on an article with many comments; query count for POST comment
validation.expectation: POST comment no longer reads existing comments
validation.falsifier: SQL log already shows no comments read on POST

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Comment threads and tag lists are often small, and the spec does not require pagination.

alternatives.option: Query comments directly and skip loading all comments in Create (preferred, spec-compatible)
alternatives.why: removes avoidable work without an API change

findings.problem: Serilog is configured at MinimumLevel.Verbose with a themed console sink and no configuration override, so every request and EF command is written to the console.
findings.performance_principle: Per-request instrumentation must have bounded, configurable cost and must not sit on the request path at maximum verbosity.

evidence.statement: MinimumLevel.Verbose() with only a Console sink; the code comment says 'just for local debug' but the method is called unconditionally.
AddSerilogLogging is invoked in Program.cs startup with no environment check and no use of appsettings.
The Dockerfile/docker-compose deploy path runs the same binary.

findings.conditions: Matters when the app runs outside local debugging at meaningful request rates (assumed); console throughput and container log capture cost are unmeasured.

counter_evidence.statement: The comment indicates local-debug intent; no environment gate was found anyway.

findings.recommendation: Read the minimum level from configuration (Information or Warning by default), override EF and Microsoft.AspNetCore namespaces to Warning, and use an async sink for production.

validation.metric: Log events per request and p95 latency with level Verbose vs Warning under the same load
validation.expectation: Lower latency and CPU at Warning

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: For a demo app at low traffic the logging cost is small and the verbosity is arguably desirable.

findings.problem: The mediator pipeline calls BeginTransaction for every message and commits afterwards, using synchronous Begin/Commit calls, so reads pay extra round trips and hold a connection for the whole handler.
findings.performance_principle: Do not pay coordination cost (transactions, connection holding) for operations that need no atomicity.

evidence.statement: Behavior registered globally for all requests.
Database.BeginTransaction (sync) and Commit (sync) in ConduitContext.

findings.conditions: Noticeable on SQL Server with network latency where BEGIN/COMMIT are extra round trips; on local SQLite it is cheap. Pool size is default and unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: In-memory provider skips the transaction; SQLite default is local so cost is small.

findings.recommendation: Apply the transaction behavior only to command handlers (marker interface), and use async BeginTransactionAsync/CommitAsync.
findings.trade_offs: Read handlers lose a shared snapshot unless a snapshot isolation level is chosen.

validation.metric: DB round trips per GET request
validation.expectation: Two fewer round trips per read on SQL Server
validation.falsifier: Provider logs show no BEGIN/COMMIT on reads

findings.problem: Create does a FindAsync per tag and a SaveChangesAsync for each new tag, then probes AnyAsync for slugs in a loop, so a single create costs O(tags + slug collisions) round trips.
findings.performance_principle: Batch writes and lookups; avoid per-item round trips for variable-size input.

evidence.statement: foreach tag: FindAsync, then AddAsync + SaveChangesAsync when missing.
for loop with AnyAsync per candidate slug, unindexed (see PERF-001).

findings.conditions: Matters for creates with many tags or many same-titled articles; write rate unknown and likely much lower than reads.

counter_evidence.statement: Tag count is client-controlled but typically small; no cap found in the validator.

findings.recommendation: Load existing tags with one Where(Contains) query, add all missing tags and the article in a single SaveChanges, and rely on a unique Slug index plus retry instead of a probe loop.
findings.trade_offs: Concurrent creates of the same new tag need conflict handling.

validation.metric: Statements per POST /api/articles with N tags
validation.expectation: Constant instead of growing with N
validation.falsifier: SQL log shows a constant statement count already

alternatives.option: Batch tag lookup and single save (preferred)

considered_not_reported.observation: Password hashing is a single HMACSHA512 pass, cheap in CPU and not a throughput concern
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: No performance impact (it is a security weakness, see SEC-001)
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: If a slow KDF is adopted, re-assess login CPU cost

considered_not_reported.observation: Feed query builds a Contains over a followed-id subquery
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Translated as a SQL subquery bounded by the follow list; no evidence of a problem
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Users following very large numbers of people

adjacent_findings.problem: The JWT signing key is a hard-coded string, and passwords are hashed with a single HMAC-SHA512 pass using a hard-coded key rather than a password KDF, so tokens can be forged by anyone with the source and hashes are cheap to brute-force.

evidence.statement: Hard-coded signing key literal in AddJwt
HMACSHA512 with constant key, single pass

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Load the signing key from secret configuration and use a password KDF (PBKDF2/Argon2/bcrypt) with per-user salt and work factor.
adjacent_findings.assessed_properly_by: A dedicated security review of authentication and secret handling
